newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says don't cut Zaire rescue mission force.
newsitem.headline: Canada says don't cut Zaire rescue mission force.

text.p: Canada, claiming partial credit on Friday for the return to Rwanda of a mass of its refugees, said it would be wrong now to cut the size of the planned international rescue mission to Central Africa.

"The initiative that was taken this week, beginning last weekend with the (Canadian) prime minister (Jean Chretien), is already I think beginning to pay its own dividends in terms of having a breakthrough," Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said.
Axworthy told a news conference that the imminent arrival of the mission had created the conditions for the return of the refugees, one of the ultimate goals for ending the refugee problem.
"The fact that the force can now be there to further enhance and support that movement really allows us to tackle something that many people only a few days ago thought was intractable," he said.
He said that while the mission might now place more emphasis on resettlement of refugees in Rwanda, a strong show of force was still needed in the area.

"I don't think you want to dilute your efforts in any way now," the minister said, noting that airports in eastern Zaire needed to be secured and safe corridors provided for the hundreds of thousands of refugees remaining.

"We still have to show a very strong presence there. Otherwise you might lose the good effect that had already been created by the fact that the force has come together and has indicated its intention to be there."
Chretien personally spearheaded the creation of the force, offering Canadian leadership and phoning leaders around the world to end U.N. delays.
He was trying to read a novel at his Harrington Lake retreat outside Ottawa last Saturday when he became disturbed by television pictures of the refugees, his spokeswoman Leslie Swartman said.

He began calling phoning around the world -- from South African President Nelson Mandela to Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso -- and his aides laid the groundwork for a conversation with President Bill Clinton.
Chretien finally talked with him on Monday morning, a few hours before Clinton made the crucial announcement that Washington would agree in principle to participate.
The sudden refugee exodus has delighted planners, who are still scrambling to look at who has gone, who is left, and what the new needs are.

Canadian defense spokesman Capt. Jocelyn Laroche said 24 soldiers had left Canada on Thursday and Friday to reconnoiter the area, in three C-130 Hercules transport planes loaded mainly with equipment.
Three more Hercules are to leave on Saturday with equipment and an Airbus with 120 reconnaissance personnel are to fly out on Sunday.

The first troops were due to start providing intelligence to Ottawa by Saturday morning. Officials said the mission's Canadian commander, Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, was likely to spend much of the weekend planning on the basis of this.
Axworthy said one idea was to have U.N.-sponsored, protected way stations acting as a magnet to draw refugees along the route back home.
He added that while the force would not separate the Hutu militiamen from the refugees, no one with guns would be granted assistance in resettlement.

Axworthy said 150,000 to 200,000 refugees may have crossed the borders on Friday, and that while others were en route, approximately 400,000 had fled west away from Rwanda, dispersing deeper into Zaire from camps around the eastern Zairean town of Goma.
